`src/sort.rs` in the fixture (`/home/projects/ulwbench-home/tmp-new/ulw-bench-S6-r1-ox4dJx`) implements quicksort with the Lomuto partition scheme. Its worst case is O(n²) time.

**Source:** `quicksort<T: Ord>` in `src/sort.rs` always picks the last element, `arr[len-1]`, as the pivot. `partition` scans once with `arr[j] <= pivot`, then swaps the pivot into position `i`. It recurses on both sides, with no random or median-of-three pivot.

**Worst case:** O(n²) time. The doc comment in the file says the same. It happens whenever the last element is repeatedly the minimum or maximum of its slice, which leaves one side empty and the other with n−1 elements. That gives about n(n−1)/2 comparisons. Average and best cases are O(n log n).

**Inputs that trigger it:** the comment lists sorted and reverse-sorted input. It misses all-equal input. Because the partition uses `<=`, every element goes to the left side, so an all-equal slice degrades the same way.

**Space:** the worst case also makes the recursion depth O(n). On a large adversarial input that risks a stack overflow, not just slowness.

**Verification:** I compiled the file's `quicksort` with `rustc` 1.98.0 in a scratch directory (`/tmp/sortverify`) and counted `Ord::cmp` calls. The repo is untouched.

| n | random | sorted | reverse | all-equal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 500 | 5,218 | 124,750 | 124,750 | 124,750 |
| 1000 | 11,160 | 499,500 | 499,500 | 499,500 |
| 2000 | 25,370 | 1,999,000 | 1,999,000 | 1,999,000 |

The three degenerate inputs match n(n−1)/2 exactly, and random input stays near n log n.

I shortened the ulw-research run. This was a one-file question, so I skipped the team and expansion waves. I also skipped the inline HTML report page, since it would only repeat a single fact.
